newsitem.title: USA: Dole listens to America, cites liberal "friends".
newsitem.headline: Dole listens to America, cites liberal "friends".

text.p: Bob Dole calls them "Listening to America" meetings, where he takes questions from "real people," but most seem to feature adoring Republican fans dishing out flattery.

The Republican presidential nominee uses a town meeting format more often now in an effort to energise a campaign mired in weak poll ratings with only six weeks left to catch President Clinton before the Nov. 5 election.
The encounters are so arranged that Dole is usually surrounded by people who ask about favourite subjects, such as his proposal to cut income tax rates by 15 percent.
That was the case in this north-central Ohio farm community where several hundred people gathered at a vocational school on Tuesday and peppered him with fluffy questions.

Typical was his first interrogator, who described herself as an educator, said "this is indeed an honour" and asked about one of Dole's favourite political targets, the liberal-oriented teachers' unions.

Dole batted that one out of the park, taking a swipe at the National Education Association -- the nation's biggest teachers' union and an old nemesis, which he claims gives 99 percent of its contributions to Democrat Clinton. He portrayed himself as a champion of teachers, as opposed to their unions, and said his education plans were "teacher friendly."
The next man asked him to explain his tax cut, a chore Dole relished as he replied at great length "This is not a Wall Street tax. This is a Main Street tax," he said.

Another woman wanted to know how he would pay for school vouchers, a Republican-favoured scheme that would help parents send their children to private schools of their choice. Dole devoured that one as well, saying he would free up some of the funds by abolishing the federal Department of Education.
And so it went, one "soft-ball" query after another sailing in from a uniformly friendly crowd.

Dole's new efforts to take the offensive against Clinton include regular efforts to paint him as "an old-style, dyed-in-the-wool, big-spending liberal" -- as he put it at one rally in Detroit on Tuesday.
Yet, the Kansas conservative also regularly lists some of the most liberal of liberals as his "friends."

That includes Sen. Edward Kennedy, the Massachusetts Democrat widely regarded as the dean of Washington liberals and proud of it. Dole, who retired as Senate majority leader last spring after 35 years in Congress, regularly cites Kennedy in his speeches as an example of a liberal Democratic taxer.

But he also calls Kennedy his "friend," an honorific also bestowed on such well-known traditional liberals as New York Sen. Pat Moynihan, the late Democratic Sen. Phil Hart of Michigan and the late Vice President Hubert Humphrey, an enduring symbol of American liberalism.

Dole, known as a collegial compromiser in the clubby Senate and ill at ease with the personal-attack politics he must now practice, insists on making the point that Clinton and the rest are his opponents but not his enemies.
Wherever he goes, Dole attracts his own crowd of Republican "paparazzi" -- men, women and youngsters who strive to snap photos of him as if he was a visiting movie star.
And he is a willing participant in these picture-taking sessions with crowds pressing the ropes at his appearances.
He even sometimes offers one of those cardboard throwaway cameras to those who lack their own, as he did in Shelby, where dozens of fans waited to shake his hand and get a photo.
"We'll just take the picture and give you the camera," he told an elderly couple. "We've got plenty of those."
